articles.summary: Hey, Carrie . . . Why Did PM2.5 Go Up Across the Region Just Ahead of the Fourth of July Weekend? If you noticed PM2.5 concentrations trending upward across the region during the recent stretch of extreme heat leading into the Fourth of July weekend, you weren’t imagining things. One of the biggest reasons was the presence of a “heat dome” — a large area of high pressure that settled over much of the eastern United States and created stagnant atmospheric conditions that allowed pollutants to accumulate near the ground. First Things First: What Is a Heat Dome? A heat dome forms when a strong high-pressure system becomes established over a region and remains in place for several days. Air beneath the high pressure slowly sinks, creating a stable atmosphere that suppresses vertical air movement and limits ventilation. Think of it as placing a lid on a pot. Under normal conditions, the atmosphere does a pretty good job of mixing and dispersing pollutants. During a heat dome, that natural mixing process slows down, causing pollutants to become trapped closer to the surface. Why Does PM2.5 Increase? PM2.5 consists of microscopic particles that are small enough to remain suspended in the atmosphere for extended periods. Under normal meteorological conditions, wind and atmospheric mixing help dilute and transport these particles away from their sources. During a heat dome, however, several things happen: Winds are often lighter, reducing pollutant dispersion. Vertical mixing is suppressed, allowing particles to remain concentrated near the ground. Emissions from vehicles, industrial facilities, power generation, construction activities, and other routine sources continue to enter the atmosphere day after day. Smoke, haze, and other fine particles have fewer opportunities to disperse and can build up across larger geographic areas. The result is often a gradual increase in PM2.5 concentrations across an entire region rather than a sharp spike at a single location. In many cases, emissions themselves have not increased significantly; instead, the atmosphere has become less efficient at “cleaning itself,” allowing particles to accumulate over time. How Long Do Heat Domes Last? Unlike a passing storm system, heat domes can be remarkably persistent. Most heat domes last anywhere from three to seven days, although stronger events can remain in place for a week or even several weeks before a change in the weather pattern breaks them down. The recent heat dome covering southwestern Pennsylvania lasted from around June 25 to July 3, with some lingering effects into July 4. ​ This is important from an air quality perspective because pollutant levels can gradually build over the life of the event. The longer stagnant conditions persist: The more pollutants accumulate near the surface. The less effective the atmosphere becomes at dispersing emissions. Overnight temperature inversions can further trap pollutants until daytime heating allows some mixing to occur. The Bottom Line The elevated PM2.5 concentrations observed during the recent heat event were largely driven by meteorology. A persistent heat dome created hot, stagnant conditions that reduced atmospheric mixing and ventilation, allowing fine particulate matter to accumulate across the region. Emissions from everyday sources continued to enter the atmosphere, but the atmosphere itself became much less effective at dispersing them. Context Corner Takeaway When a heat dome settles over the region, think of it as placing a lid on the atmosphere. Even when emissions remain relatively steady, PM2.5 concentrations can increase because pollutants become trapped near the ground and accumulate day after day. The longer the heat dome lingers, the greater the opportunity for that buildup to occur. In many cases, what we’re observing isn’t necessarily an increase in emissions, it’s a decrease in the atmosphere’s ability to disperse them. articles.summary: CNX Resources Corporation reported another quarter of durable performance in the second quarter of 2026, generating $138 million in free cash flow and marking its 26th consecutive quarter of positive free cash flow generation. Since the inception of its seven-year plan in 2020, CNX’s differentiated business model has now produced approximately $3.1 billion in cumulative free cash flow. “Q2 2026 marks our 26th consecutive quarter of free cash flow generation, highlighting our Sustainable Business Model that is the cornerstone of our success,” said Alan Shepard, President and CEO. “During the quarter, we opportunistically repurchased a significant number of shares and reduced our total debt outstanding. The strength of our balance sheet, combined with our consistent cash flow generation, provides significant flexibility as we continue to clinically allocate capital to grow long-term per share value.” That flexibility shows in how CNX allocated capital during the quarter. CNX repurchased approximately 5.6 million shares for $199 million at an average price of $35.28 per share, and after quarter-end bought back another 1.2 million shares for $40 million at an average price of $33.03 per share. Since its peak share count in the third quarter of 2020, the company has now repurchased about 106 million shares for $2.2 billion at an average price of $20.43 per share — a market-leading 34 percent cumulative reduction in shares outstanding. On the balance sheet side, CNX retired the remaining $209 million of its outstanding convertible notes during the quarter, settling the obligation by issuing approximately 12.6 million shares net of the capped call settlement. Combined with the quarter’s activity, CNX has reduced net debt by $193 million year-to-date. Behind the financial results was another quarter of steady operational execution. The team drilled 2 Utica Shale wells in Central Pennsylvania (CPA), frac’d 6 Marcellus Shale wells in Southwestern Pennsylvania (SWPA), and turned in line [1] 5 SWPA Marcellus wells during the quarter. CNX also set a new company record for 24-hour lateral footage drilled in the Utica, reaching 4,416 feet. Given current commodity market conditions, the company continues to run a maintenance-of-production program of roughly 1.5 rigs and a partial-year fracturing crew, with capital expenditures expected to rise in the third quarter before declining in the fourth, and production volumes expected to peak in the fourth quarter. Above: Mentorship Academy participants touring CNX operations this past April. CNX’s lower-carbon product platform also continued to contribute to results. The company recognized about $13 million in net sales of environmental attributes tied to approximately 4.0 Bcf [2] of Remediated Mine Gas (RMG) [3] during the quarter, keeping it on pace for its full-year target of roughly 17 Bcf of RMG and about $50 million in Pennsylvania Tier 1 Alternative Energy Credit (AEC) [4] net sales at current market prices. After quarter-end, CNX also sold credits under Section 45Z [5] of the federal tax code for approximately $30 million in net cash proceeds — a $10 million increase from prior guidance — after the U.S. Treasury clarified that the company’s 2025 remediation activities qualified for a full year of monetization. A subsequent U.S. Department of Energy update to the emissions-modeling formula used to calculate those credits is expected to push total annual 45Z tax credit sales to approximately $40 million beginning in 2027. Looking ahead, CNX reaffirmed its 2026 production guidance of 605 to 620 Bcfe [6], with 34 total wells expected to turn in line (27 Marcellus, 7 deep Utica), and reaffirmed base capital expenditure guidance of $540 million to $570 million. Using a natural gas price of $3.55 per MMBtu [7] based on July 15 NYMEX [8] pricing, the company continues to expect approximately $525 million of full-year free cash flow, with free cash flow per share guidance rising from $3.41 to $3.55 per share following the quarter’s buybacks. On the environmental, social, and governance front, CNX’s industry-leading Radical Transparency program surpassed 1.1 million air quality datapoints collected since inception, with the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection now leveraging the public-private program to conduct an independent greenfield site monitoring study in Washington County — one of the most intensive studies of unconventional gas wells undertaken in the country. As with prior monitoring, CNX continues to find no evidence that its gas development operations harm human health or degrade local air quality, a track record that calls into question proposals for expanded buffer zones in Pennsylvania. Taken together, the second quarter reflected a familiar CNX formula: disciplined operations, another quarter of free cash flow generation, continued share repurchases, a stronger balance sheet, and ongoing investment in lower-carbon products and transparent operations. For Appalachia, that’s another quarter of pairing energy production with long-term, per share value creation. For more, read CNX’s full Q2 2026 prepared remarks, review the accompanying earnings presentation, read the full results and supplemental information, and visit CNX’s news page for the latest company announcements. Notes “Turned in line” means a well has been completed and connected for sales. Bcf = billion cubic feet, a standard unit for measuring natural gas volume. RMG is natural gas captured from mine ventilation systems that would otherwise be released into the atmosphere. AECs are credits generated under Pennsylvania’s Alternative Energy Portfolio Standard for qualifying energy sources. Section 45Z is a federal tax credit for producing lower-carbon transportation fuels. Bcfe = billion cubic feet equivalent, a unit that converts natural gas and related liquids into one comparable measure. MMBtu = million British thermal units, the standard unit used to price natural gas. NYMEX = New York Mercantile Exchange, where natural gas futures prices are set.
